Yet the forces responsible for social oppression could also benefit from a belief that justice would be postponed until the next world.
3 — Islam did not stop at principles of belief. It also introduced a system of law in which the social effects were much clearer than they were in the religious doctrines themselves.
Islamic law prohibited usury, monopoly, and the hoarding of gold and silver.
It imposed the zakāt tax on certain forms of wealth belonging to the rich and made its proceeds the right of particular groups among the poorest and most needy.
It also introduced rules regulating certain productive and social relationships.
Yet the basic principle of Islamic law still accepted social differentiation.
Even so, these laws came as a shock to the wealthy people of Mecca and spread alarm among them.

They looked at what an Islamic victory might do to their immediate interests. They did not yet have enough class awareness to see that, over the longer term, the general direction of development would not conflict with the development of their own class position.
For this reason, Islam, Muhammad, and the first Muslims faced violent persecution from the wealthy Qurayshi leadership in Mecca.
At the beginning of the Islamic movement, however, Islam did not win many supporters among the poor of Mecca either.
The social laws we have described did not appear until after the migration from Mecca to Medina.
For these poor people, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment on the Day of Resurrection were not enough reason to endure persecution in defence of Islam.
They needed an immediate material answer to their material problems.
4 — Islam also introduced ideas about the metaphysical nature of the universe and the world, about the place of human beings within the universe, and about human responsibility for their actions.

Yet the Qur’an appears contradictory when it comes to defining this responsibility. At some points it presents human beings as free in their actions, while at others it speaks in terms of compulsion and predestination.

5 — In Chapter Two, we also examined the Muslim migration from Mecca to Medina, or Yathrib, along with its causes, its decisive consequences, and the conflict between Mecca and Medina that followed it.

Throughout this conflict, the basic issue remained the same: the changes that the Islamic movement was bringing to the social forms that had dominated pre-Islamic society, especially the society of Mecca.
6 — We then examined the legislative stage of Islam, which began immediately after the migration to Medina.
We saw that the laws introduced during this stage were grounded, for the most part, in material conditions and were closely connected to the practical needs created by the migration itself.
Later, they were also shaped by the victories that the Anṣār and Muhājirūn began to win against the Qurayshi leadership in Mecca.
Eventually that leadership accepted the new reality.
Mecca came under Islam and returned to its position as a religious centre, but now in a new form and under the banner of Islam.
While discussing Islamic law in this chapter, we also pointed to an important feature of its development: the existence of a principle allowing law to change and develop.

This stands in contrast to the later belief, common among some Muslim scholars, that everything laid down by Islamic law is permanent until the Day of Resurrection and may never be changed or altered.
7 — In trying to define a “theory” of knowledge in Islam, we found that knowledge was ultimately traced back to a divine source: revelation from God to the Prophet.
This applied whether the knowledge concerned religious belief or law.
Knowledge therefore became tied to faith.

We based this account of the “theory” of knowledge, and of the relationship between knowledge and religious faith, on Islam’s basic sources: the Qur’an and the Sunna, meaning the sayings and actions of the Prophet.
On this basis, we found that rational debate was not accepted by the Prophet. In fact, he rejected it and called on people to avoid it, especially in questions of religious belief.
We based this conclusion on Qur’anic verses, on hadiths transmitted from the Prophet by his companions, and on the views of both early and later Muslim scholars.
In this connection, we observed that the rejection of rational debate over matters of belief created a certain break in the historical development of Arab thought.
But this was not an absolute break.
An absolute break in any process of historical development, whatever the subject, would contradict the law of development itself—and development is the only absolute law.
We therefore saw that Arab thought, during this period of its history, opened another path for itself, different from the one it had been following shortly before Islam appeared.
It found this path through the use of reasoned judgment, or ijtihād al-raʾy, when applying general legal rules to new situations, events, and needs in Muslim life.
This form of ijtihād created some room for rational thought, even if that room remained limited.
In the chapters ahead, however, we will see that the development of Arab thought did not remain confined within these narrow limits.
From the end of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the beginning of the Umayyad period, it began to move along several different paths.

8 — Once we had concluded that Islam’s “theory” of knowledge ultimately traced knowledge back to a divine source, we also had to examine the Qur’anic verses and prophetic hadiths that call on people “to use reason and to praise the gift of reason.”
Here we observed that the context of these texts limits the value of reason to what it can contribute in support of religious, faith-based knowledge.
Even so, we found something positive in the attention that both the Qur’an and the Sunna give to reason, even within these limits.
They recognize that religious beliefs themselves need the support of reason.
We then traced the different sides of this question back to the fact that they reflected an objective reality that could not simply be ignored.
9 — Finally, at the end of the chapter, we discussed the other cultural developments that appeared during this stage in the history of Islam.
We noted a certain decline in Arabic poetry alongside the growth of public speaking.

We explained this partly by Islam’s struggle against poetry and its attempt to direct people’s attention toward the highly developed Qur’anic style and its artistic and aesthetic qualities, in addition to the Qur’an’s religious and legal content.

A — The Social and Political Conflict Erupts
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, the founder of Islam, died in Medina in 632 CE, twenty-two years after he began his mission. He spent the first thirteen of those years in Mecca and the remaining years in Medina after the Hijra. He is generally said to have been born in 570 CE, which would mean that he lived for sixty-two years.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

His death came as a severe shock to Muslims in general. But for some of them, it caused something deeper. They had come to see Muhammad, as a prophet, as somehow standing above ordinary human nature. In their minds, he could not simply die as other human beings did.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
For a few moments, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb seems to have reacted in this way. When he saw people mourning Muhammad, he quickly went to the pulpit of the mosque and addressed them:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

“I do not want to hear anyone say that Muhammad has died. He has only been summoned away, just as Moses son of ʿImrān was summoned away and remained absent from his people for forty nights... By God, I expect that the hands and feet of men who claim that he has died will be cut off.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Abū Bakr then arrived while ʿUmar was still speaking. He told him to be quiet, and ʿUmar stopped. Abū Bakr climbed the pulpit and said:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“As for what follows: whoever among you worshipped Muhammad should know that Muhammad has died. But whoever worships God should know that God is living and never dies.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Muhammad is only a messenger. Other messengers passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?...”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar asked, “Is this in the Book of God?”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
According to another account, ʿUmar later said:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“By God, as soon as I heard Abū Bakr recite it, my legs gave way beneath me while I was still standing. I fell to the ground and knew with certainty that the Prophet had died.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

This shock occurred even though Muhammad had never misled people about his human nature. Through the Qur’an and through his own words, he had repeatedly stressed that he was a human being like other human beings.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

But another image had taken hold in people’s minds. Muhammad was connected with divine revelation. The Qur’an was seen as miraculous. And people believed that Muhammad himself was illiterate and could neither read nor write. Together, these ideas planted the belief that the Prophet possessed a nature higher than that of ordinary human beings. Some therefore found it difficult to accept that death could reach him just as it reached everyone else.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Abū Bakr’s firm and direct intervention settled the matter. It brought back to reality those who had surrendered to this illusion, whether because they lacked understanding or because their social position gave them an interest in presenting Islam as something above ordinary human reality.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As soon as the Prophet’s death was announced, the leading Companions among the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār began to struggle over political power.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The struggle started immediately, before the Prophet’s body had even been taken to its final resting place in Medina. It also divided his Companions into two groups: the Muhājirūn, the emigrants from Mecca, and the Anṣār, the people of Medina who had supported them. Each group wanted control of the caliphate after the Prophet. In other words, each wanted actual leadership of the new political authority.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This division suddenly brought back to the surface old tensions between Mecca and Medina. Those tensions had been suppressed for only a few years under the authority of the single Islamic community.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

At the same time, early class-like tensions between the Anṣār and the Muhājirūn also began to appear openly. These feelings had existed before, but they had not come fully into the open during the Prophet’s lifetime.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

In the first years after the Hijra, a new Islamic organization had taken shape in Medina. It resembled a kind of communal order. It stood above the tribe, and Islam as a religion provided the framework that held the whole community together.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In principle, this made it different from the older forms of primitive communal life, where tribal loyalty had been the basis of unity.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Yet even within this new Islamic organization, there was a clear difference between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār. The Muhājirūn formed its leading group. They received the larger share of war booty, and the organization was largely led by their own prominent figures, especially Abū Bakr and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. These two men appeared to play the leading role in managing its affairs.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

This created a certain disappointment among the leaders of the Anṣār, who were the original inhabitants of Medina. They had invited Muhammad and his Meccan followers to migrate to their city and had supported the Islamic cause. They had expected more from this relationship.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

They carried this disappointment within them and kept it under control throughout Muhammad’s life in Medina. But as soon as the news spread that Muhammad had died, those suppressed feelings came rapidly to the surface.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
At the same time, another division appeared among the Muhājirūn themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Old differences from the pre-Islamic period came back to life between the Banū Hāshim, the clan of the Prophet and of his cousin and son-in-law ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, on one side, and the Banū ʿAbd Shams, Taym, Umayya, and the other Quraysh clans to which the rest of the Muhājirūn belonged, including Abū Bakr and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, on the other.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Most of the Banū Hāshim had represented the poorer branch among the leading clans of Quraysh in pre-Islamic Mecca. It was therefore natural that, after losing the Prophet, they should think about how to preserve the position they had gained through him.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Muhammad had been the greatest expression of that position. Indeed, he had given it its highest meaning.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The Banū Hāshim could now try to preserve that position through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law. ʿAlī had fought courageously at Muhammad’s side in the wars against the leaders of Mecca after the Hijra. And on the night Muhammad left Mecca for Medina, ʿAlī had slept in his bed, exposing himself to the plot that Quraysh had prepared to kill Muhammad before he could escape.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
All these factors caused the struggle to erupt immediately after the Prophet’s death.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

One striking feature is that the people involved did not manage to hide the real political and social motives behind the conflict beneath a religious appearance. Muslim historians themselves describe the events quite openly. In brief, this is the picture they give us.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

While ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet’s uncle, and Usāma ibn Zayd, one of the Companions, were washing and preparing the Prophet’s body for burial, then carrying it to the place near the room where he had died in the house of his wife ʿĀʾisha, a spokesman for the Anṣār called out to the Muhājirūn:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Give us a share in the Messenger of God in his death, just as we had a share in him during his life.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

At first, this seemed to mean only that the Anṣār wanted to take part in the burial so that they too could have the honor of participating. ʿAlī therefore immediately invited one of the Anṣār, Aws ibn Khawlī, to go down into the grave with them and help bury the Prophet and say the final farewell.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But the meaning of the word “share” soon became clearer.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

While ʿAlī was inviting Aws to take part in the burial, the leaders of the Anṣār were meeting at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida. There they declared the Khazraj leader Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda to be ruler of the Muslims—that is, caliph after Muhammad.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

When Abū Bakr, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and some of the other Muhājirūn heard what was happening, they hurried to the meeting place. They moved the crowd away from Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda, whom the Anṣār had proclaimed their leader, and Abū Bakr made his way to the front of the gathering.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“People of the Anṣār! The Messenger of God is from us, so we have the stronger claim to take his place.”
